reason: The text emphasizes hierarchy through multiple explicit markers: Jacob repeatedly uses master/servant language (calling Esau 'my master'/אֲדֹנִי and himself 'your servant'/עַבְדְּךָ), physically bows down seven times before approaching Esau, and strategically arranges his wives and children in a hierarchical order—placing the servants and their children first, then Leah and her children, then Rachel and Joseph last. Jacob presents gifts as tribute to a superior. The narrative presents this hierarchical approach not critically but as the successful means to achieve reconciliation, implicitly endorsing submission to hierarchy as appropriate and effective.
